As a group, women tend to respond better and to require lower dosages
than men. Unfortunately, there are no biologic or clinical indicators that
can be used to predict treatment response other than the patient’s prior
responses.

Some of the dopamine D2 receptor antagonists are represented among
the first group of effective agents for schizophrenia and other psychotic
illnesses. They include fluphenazine, haloperidol, amisulpride, pimozide,
and perphenazine. Although many of these drugs have gradually been
replaced by dopamine–serotonin, serotonin–dopamine, and serotonin–
dopamine–norepinephrine antagonists in the United States, dopamine
antagonists remain the most commonly prescribed antipsychotics in many
parts of the world, and as cost considerations have become more
prominent, dopamine D2 receptor antagonists remain frequently
prescribed in the United States as well.
These agents are highly effective for nearly all disorders that result in
psychotic symptoms. However, these drugs have important limitations:
They can cause acute and chronic neurologic symptoms that, especially
at higher doses, significantly limit their effectiveness; they are ineffective
or only partially effective for a substantial proportion of psychotic patients;
the minimally effective dosage has frequently not been determined, and
therefore patients may be over-or undermedicated; and they have limited
efficacy for some of the most important signs and symptoms of the most
common psychotic illness, schizophrenia. In higher dosages, the motor
symptoms may induce “secondary” negative symptoms, such as akinesia,
emotional blunting, apathy, and cognitive impairment.

EUFEST compared several dopamine–serotonin blockers, olanzapine,
quetiapine, ziprasidone with a low dose (1 to 4 mg) of the high-potency
Dopamine D2 blockers haloperidol and amisulpride in the treatment of
first-episode schizophrenia. The pragmatic trial found high-discontinuation
rates

and
rehospitalization rates were virtually the same in all groups. Alongside
olanzapine, amisulpride had the lowest rates of discontinuation for any
reason across an entire year. The results of these trials do not mean that
older and newer antipsychotics are equivalent in their side-effect profiles.
The differences in EPS liability may have been underestimated in CATIE.
First, eliminating patients with evidence of TD may have excluded those
who were most vulnerable to discomforting EPS side effects. Moreover,
while there were no differences in EPS ratings for parkinsonism and
akathisia between perphenazine and the SGAs, it is interesting to note
that the higher rate of discontinuations for EPS among the perphenazine-
treated patients suggests that ratings may not have been adequately
sensitive. However, most of the studies documenting large differences
between these drugs may have used what would now be considered
excessive doses of haloperidol, a drug with an incidence of EPS, which
may have exaggerated the difference between the two types of agents.
The current body evidence does not support the earlier belief that the
dopamine–serotonin or dopamine–serotonin–norepinephrine blockers are
more effective than dopamine D2 blockers. However, the dopamine D2
blockers are more likely to cause EPS and, as noted below, are probably
more likely to cause TD. Perhaps dopamine D2 blockers should be
prescribed in lower dosages than historical uses. If patients are treated
with dopamine D2 blockers, they should be regularly monitored for EPS,
particularly drug-induced parkinsonism and akathisia, and they should be
assessed for evidence of TD.
Maintenance Treatment in Schizophrenia and Schizoaffective
Disorders
Dopamine D2 blockers are effective in decreasing the risk of psychotic
relapse in patients who have recovered from a psychotic episode.
National and international guidelines indicate that after the acute phase of
treatment for a first episode, treatment should continue for at least 1 year,
but there is no consensus regarding the total duration of treatment, if the
patient remains symptomatic. In case of multiple episodes, maintenance

These agents, in themselves quite heterogeneous, have different side-
effect profiles when compared with dopamine blockers. The most
important advantage of these “newer agents” is that they cause
substantially less EPS. Patients who experience EPS at dosages of
dopamine blocker needed to treat their psychosis may or may not
experience EPS with an effective dosage of any of these other agents.
This was evaluated in a phase of the CATIE trial in which patients who
discontinued perphenazine were subsequently randomized to risperidone,
olanzapine, or quetiapine.
There is also evidence from a number of well-designed clinical trials
indicating that patients who have only partial responses to a dopamine
blocker due to lack of efficacy or side effects may improve, if changed to a
dopamine–serotonin and dopamine–serotonin–norepinephrine antagonist.
The evidence is compelling for clozapine, but there are also some reports
supportive of other agents as well. However, most of the studies reporting
this advantage of newer drugs were carried out in the late 1980s and
1990s when patients had only been exposed to dopamine D2 blockers.
More recently, there are clinical reports of patients who had only received
dopamine–serotonin or dopamine–serotonin–norepinephrine antagonists
who improved when they were changed to a dopamine D2 blocker.
Moreover, cost considerations have become more important, especially in
the United States. Many of the newer medications are patent protected
and are considerably more expensive than dopamine blockers which are
usually available as generics. Risks and benefits need to be considered
carefully when choosing antipsychotics, especially in light of the different
TD risks.
An additional advantage of some newer medications is that they are
less likely to elevate prolactin. As a result, these agents may be helpful for
women who experience galactorrhea and irregular menses with dopamine
blockers.
Haloperidol and fluphenazine are still commonly prescribed. They are
more strongly antidopaminergic and thus more likely to cause EPS than
other available medications. However, EPS in some individuals may be
easier to manage than the sedation and orthostatic hypotension
associated with other medications. Haloperidol and Prolixin can also
readily be administered intramuscularly and seldom cause problems with

considerably. For many patients, dopamine D2 blockers can lead to a
complete remission of psychotic symptoms. The early studies from the
NIMH indicate that 60% of drug-treated patients improved to the extent
that they achieved a complete remission (albeit temporarily) or
experienced only mild symptoms; the remaining 40% will continue to
experience psychotic symptoms, and approximately 8% of them are not
improved with drug treatment. A comprehensive meta-analysis published
in 2019 in JAMA that compared 32 oral antipsychotics showed that
amisulpride was the second most effective antipsychotic at reducing
overall symptoms in schizophrenia patients (behind clozapine) and the
most effective in terms of reducing positive symptoms. The analysis also
ranked amisulpride better than clozapine in terms of tolerability and side
effects.
Positive psychotic symptoms, which include hallucinations and
delusions, are more responsive to dopamine D2 receptor antagonists than
are negative symptoms, such as blunted affect, emotional withdrawal, and
lack of social or vocational interest, or disorganized symptoms, such as
impaired attention and impaired communication. Although these latter two
groups of symptoms are less responsive than psychotic symptoms,
double-blind studies indicate that these symptoms improve to some
degree. Amisulpride, at lower doses, tends to stimulate rather than block
dopamine release, producing antidepressant effects, rendering it
potentially useful for the treatment of schizophrenia patients with negative
symptoms. EPS can cause secondary negative symptoms, compounding
symptom burden. Patients with parkinsonism may demonstrate fewer
expressive gestures and diminished interest in their environment.

than men. Unfortunately, there are no biologic or clinical indicators that
can be used to predict treatment response other than the patient’s prior
responses.

TREATMENT OF ACUTE PSYCHOSIS
Initiation of Treatment
Treatment with a dopamine blocker is usually initiated soon after a
diagnosis is made. Whenever possible, patients should receive a
psychiatric evaluation, including a history and physical examination and a
laboratory evaluation that includes complete blood cell count; blood
electrolytes; glucose, liver, renal, and thyroid function tests; and other
appropriate evaluations (including ECG, pregnancy tests, and screens for
alcohol and drugs). The results of this evaluation can be useful in
confirming the diagnosis and establishing a pretreatment baseline. Under
most conditions, it is not necessary to delay treatment while awaiting the
results of these tests. Moreover, because there are few contraindications
to receiving FGAs, these evaluations can be postponed when patients
refuse an evaluation or when treatment is urgent.
Choice of Agent
There is no evidence for differential effectiveness of dopamine D2

or

slightly lower EPS risk and does not appear to be as sedating as some of
the low-potency SGAs. The choice among the dopamine D2 blockers is
based on prior responses, both objective improvement and the patient’s
subjective response to the drug, available routes of administration and
dosage forms, side-effect profiles, and cost.

INTERPRETATION
Acute Psychosis
Numerous double-blind clinical trials have demonstrated that dopamine
D2 blockers are more effective than placebo for reducing symptoms of
psychosis. The initial studies were carried out in the 1960s by the NIMH,
reviewed by Donald Klein and John Davis, who concluded that with the
exception of mepazine (Pacatal) and promazine, all of these agents were
effective. These and subsequent studies also demonstrated that
antipsychotics are effective for every subgroup of patients with
schizophrenia. In 2009, the Schizophrenia Patient Outcomes Research
Team (PORT) updated prior reviews and concluded that there is clear
evidence that dopamine D2 blockers are effective for reducing positive
symptoms during acute psychotic episodes. PORT recommendations also
suggest that choosing antipsychotics should be based on individual
preference, prior treatment response and adherence history, medical
history and risk factors, the individual medication’s side-effect profile, and
long-term treatment planning. Studies found that amisulpride can be
safely administered at an optimal dose immediately, not needing a titration
phase and thereby aiding in acute symptom control.
Controlled clinical trials have demonstrated that dopamine D2 blockers
are effective in reducing psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations and
paranoid ideation, to a greater extent than anxiety and depression.

citations.text: EUFEST compared amisulpride with other antipsychotics in first-episode schizophrenia.
Symptom reductions and rehospitalization rates were virtually the same in all groups.
Amisulpride had among the lowest rates of discontinuation for any reason, alongside olanzapine.

answer.explanation: The Kaplan passage states that EUFEST compared olanzapine, quetiapine, ziprasidone, haloperidol, and amisulpride in first-episode schizophrenia, and that the trial found high discontinuation rates overall, with symptom reductions and rehospitalization rates virtually the same in all groups. It also notes that, alongside olanzapine, amisulpride had the lowest rates of discontinuation for any reason. This supports the conclusion that amisulpride was broadly comparable in effectiveness to the other antipsychotics, with a relatively favorable discontinuation profile in the trial.
answer.direct_answer: In EUFEST, amisulpride performed about as well as the other antipsychotics overall: symptom reduction and rehospitalization rates were virtually the same across groups, and amisulpride had among the lowest discontinuation rates, alongside olanzapine.

dopamine–serotonin or dopamine–serotonin–norepinephrine blockers are

blockers are more likely to cause EPS and, as noted below, are probably
more likely to cause TD. Perhaps dopamine D2 blockers should be

in 2019 in JAMA that compared 32 oral antipsychotics showed that

overall symptoms in schizophrenia patients (behind clozapine) and the
most effective in terms of reducing positive symptoms. The analysis also
ranked amisulpride better than clozapine in terms of tolerability and side
effects.
Positive psychotic symptoms, which include hallucinations and
delusions, are more responsive to dopamine D2 receptor antagonists than
are negative symptoms, such as blunted affect, emotional withdrawal, and
lack of social or vocational interest, or disorganized symptoms, such as
impaired attention and impaired communication. Although these latter two
groups of symptoms are less responsive than psychotic symptoms,
double-blind studies indicate that these symptoms improve to some
degree. Amisulpride, at lower doses, tends to stimulate rather than block
dopamine release, producing antidepressant effects, rendering it
potentially useful for the treatment of schizophrenia patients with negative
symptoms. EPS can cause secondary negative symptoms, compounding
symptom burden. Patients with parkinsonism may demonstrate fewer
expressive gestures and diminished interest in their environment.

been consistently shown to impair memory in patients who require these

Dopamine-serotonin antagonists (DSAs) are the most widely prescribed
agents for schizophrenia and other illnesses associated with psychotic
symptoms.
This diverse group of compounds can be differentiated from the
dopamine receptor antagonists based on their high affinity for serotonin
2A (5-HT2A) as well as dopamine (D2) receptors. In prior editions of this
text, the term second-generation antipsychotics or SGAs was used to
refer to these agents. However, this term is inaccurate since decades of
studies have failed to support the contention that antipsychotics marketed
after clozapine were more effective antipsychotics than older drugs. The
adoption of neuroscience-based nomenclature (NbN) provides a preferred
method for characterizing antipsychotic medications based on their
pharmacology. It is notable that antipsychotics previously considered first-
generation antipsychotics—including chlorpromazine, thioridazine, and
flupenthixol—are categorized as DSAs, and sulpiride and amisulpride are
classified as dopamine antagonists (DAs).
The differentiation of the DSAs from other antipsychotics emerged
following the introduction of clozapine (Clozaril), an antipsychotic that was
introduced in the United States in 1990, although it had been available in
some countries in Europe since the early 1970s. Clozapine was
considered an “atypical” antipsychotic because it was an effective agent at
doses that caused negligible extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS). Moreover,
it had broad effectiveness for a range of mood and anxiety symptoms that
were common in schizophrenia. This led to a focus on understanding the
mechanism of action of clozapine. Clozapine’s D2 receptor blockade is
lower than that of traditional antipsychotics, while its antagonism of the 5-
HT2 receptor is greater than that of haloperidol. The unique activity at
these two receptors led Herbert Meltzer to propose that the distinctive
antipsychotic effect of clozapine was related to its low receptor blockade
at D2 relative to 5-HT2. Clozapine’s affinity for the 5-HT2 receptor is
among the highest for antipsychotic agents.
During the early 1980s, scientists at Janssen Pharmaceutica were
interested in developing an antipsychotic that would have a clinical profile
similar to clozapine but without a tendency to cause agranulocytosis. The
company developed a number of drugs with 5-HT2 antagonism with and
without D2 activity. One compound, setoperone, had weak dopamine
activity and was a relatively weak antipsychotic. Ritanserin was developed

as a 5-HT2 antagonist (inverse agonist) that could be added to a D2
antagonist to decrease the amount of extrapyramidal side effects.
Although ritanserin had antinegative symptom effects, improved sleep,
and some weak antipsychotic effects, it also had significant effects on QTc
interval. The synthesis of risperidone in 1984 led the company to focus on
the development of this agent since it combined strong D2 and 5-HT2
antagonism. Subsequent safety and efficacy studies with risperidone led
to its approval in the United States in 1994. This was followed by the
introduction of olanzapine in 1996 and quetiapine in 1997, and others
during the subsequent years. This chapter will discuss the DSAs using the
following NbN categories:
1. Dopamine, serotonin (chlorpromazine, flupenthixol, loxapine,
lurasidone, olanzapine, perospirone, pipotiazine, sertindole,
thioridazine, trifluoperazine, zotepine)
2. Dopamine, serotonin NE α2 (clozapine, risperidone, paliperidone)
3. Dopamine, serotonin, NET (quetiapine)
4. Serotonin, dopamine (iloperidone)
5. Serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine (asenapine)
6. Serotonin, dopamine, serotonin transporter (lumateperone)
The partial agonists, aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, and cariprazine are
discussed in the next chapter.
Comparisons of DSAs
A network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials compared the
effectiveness of 32 antipsychotics. The study found that clozapine,
amisulpride, zotepine, olanzapine, and risperidone were more effective for
improving overall symptoms than other antipsychotics. However, with the
exception of clozapine, the differences between the drugs were relatively
small, and it was not clear that the DSAs were more effective than the
DAs. The differences among the antipsychotics in side effects were
substantial. A reasonable conclusion from this and other meta-analyses is
that—aside from clozapine—the selection of an antipsychotic will be
based on side-effect concerns rather than efficacy.
DOPAMINE, SEROTONIN

citations.text: Amisulpride is primarily a dopamine D2/D3 receptor antagonist.

answer.explanation: The evidence package describes amisulpride as a dopamine receptor antagonist. NbN specifies antagonist activity at D2 and D3 receptors and notes presynaptic D2 antagonism, with receptor occupancy data consistent with central dopamine blockade. Stahl similarly states that amisulpride theoretically blocks presynaptic dopamine D2 receptors at low doses and postsynaptic D2 receptors at higher doses, and adds that it blocks D3 receptors. Stahl also notes that amisulpride lacks potent 5-HT2A or 5-HT1A activity, but does have antagonist actions at 5-HT7 and 5-HT2B receptors, which may contribute to antidepressant effects. Dopamine-serotonin antagonists (DSAs) are the most widely prescribed
agents for schizophrenia and other illnesses associated with psychotic
symptoms.
This diverse group of compounds can be differentiated from the
dopamine receptor antagonists based on their high affinity for serotonin
2A (5-HT2A) as well as dopamine (D2) receptors. In prior editions of this
text, the term second-generation antipsychotics or SGAs was used to
refer to these agents. However, this term is inaccurate since decades of
studies have failed to support the contention that antipsychotics marketed
after clozapine were more effective antipsychotics than older drugs. The
adoption of neuroscience-based nomenclature (NbN) provides a preferred
method for characterizing antipsychotic medications based on their
pharmacology. It is notable that antipsychotics previously considered first-
generation antipsychotics—including chlorpromazine, thioridazine, and
flupenthixol—are categorized as DSAs, and sulpiride and amisulpride are
classified as dopamine antagonists (DAs).
The differentiation of the DSAs from other antipsychotics emerged
following the introduction of clozapine (Clozaril), an antipsychotic that was
introduced in the United States in 1990, although it had been available in
some countries in Europe since the early 1970s. Clozapine was
considered an “atypical” antipsychotic because it was an effective agent at
doses that caused negligible extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS). Moreover,
it had broad effectiveness for a range of mood and anxiety symptoms that
were common in schizophrenia. This led to a focus on understanding the
mechanism of action of clozapine. Clozapine’s D2 receptor blockade is
lower than that of traditional antipsychotics, while its antagonism of the 5-
HT2 receptor is greater than that of haloperidol. The unique activity at
these two receptors led Herbert Meltzer to propose that the distinctive
antipsychotic effect of clozapine was related to its low receptor blockade
at D2 relative to 5-HT2. Clozapine’s affinity for the 5-HT2 receptor is
among the highest for antipsychotic agents.
During the early 1980s, scientists at Janssen Pharmaceutica were
interested in developing an antipsychotic that would have a clinical profile
similar to clozapine but without a tendency to cause agranulocytosis. The
company developed a number of drugs with 5-HT2 antagonism with and
without D2 activity. One compound, setoperone, had weak dopamine
activity and was a relatively weak antipsychotic. Ritanserin was developed

considerably. For many patients, dopamine D2 blockers can lead to a
complete remission of psychotic symptoms. The early studies from the
NIMH indicate that 60% of drug-treated patients improved to the extent
that they achieved a complete remission (albeit temporarily) or
experienced only mild symptoms; the remaining 40% will continue to
experience psychotic symptoms, and approximately 8% of them are not
improved with drug treatment. A comprehensive meta-analysis published
in 2019 in JAMA that compared 32 oral antipsychotics showed that
amisulpride was the second most effective antipsychotic at reducing
overall symptoms in schizophrenia patients (behind clozapine) and the
most effective in terms of reducing positive symptoms. The analysis also
ranked amisulpride better than clozapine in terms of tolerability and side
effects.
Positive psychotic symptoms, which include hallucinations and
delusions, are more responsive to dopamine D2 receptor antagonists than
are negative symptoms, such as blunted affect, emotional withdrawal, and
lack of social or vocational interest, or disorganized symptoms, such as
impaired attention and impaired communication. Although these latter two
groups of symptoms are less responsive than psychotic symptoms,
double-blind studies indicate that these symptoms improve to some
degree. Amisulpride, at lower doses, tends to stimulate rather than block
dopamine release, producing antidepressant effects, rendering it
potentially useful for the treatment of schizophrenia patients with negative
symptoms. EPS can cause secondary negative symptoms, compounding
symptom burden. Patients with parkinsonism may demonstrate fewer
expressive gestures and diminished interest in their environment.

Initiation of Treatment
Treatment with a dopamine blocker is usually initiated soon after a
diagnosis is made. Whenever possible, patients should receive a
psychiatric evaluation, including a history and physical examination and a
laboratory evaluation that includes complete blood cell count; blood
electrolytes; glucose, liver, renal, and thyroid function tests; and other
appropriate evaluations (including ECG, pregnancy tests, and screens for
alcohol and drugs). The results of this evaluation can be useful in
confirming the diagnosis and establishing a pretreatment baseline. Under
most conditions, it is not necessary to delay treatment while awaiting the
results of these tests. Moreover, because there are few contraindications
to receiving FGAs, these evaluations can be postponed when patients
refuse an evaluation or when treatment is urgent.

There is no evidence for differential effectiveness of dopamine D2

dosage forms, side-effect profiles, and cost.

answer.explanation: The evidence package shows two FDA-approved indications for amisulpride, both specifically for the Barhemsys injection formulation: (1) prevention of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV), either as monotherapy or with an antiemetic from a different class, and (2) treatment of PONV in patients who received prophylaxis with an antiemetic from a different class or who did not receive prophylaxis. The package also lists schizophrenia and dysthymia as not FDA approved, and those indications are described as outside the USA or not FDA approved. This diverse group of compounds can be differentiated from the
dopamine receptor antagonists based on their high affinity for serotonin

adoption of neuroscience-based nomenclature (NbN) provides a preferred
method for characterizing antipsychotic medications based on their
pharmacology. It is notable that antipsychotics previously considered first-

flupenthixol—are categorized as DSAs, and sulpiride and amisulpride are
classified as dopamine antagonists (DAs).
The differentiation of the DSAs from other antipsychotics emerged
following the introduction of clozapine (Clozaril), an antipsychotic that was
introduced in the United States in 1990, although it had been available in
some countries in Europe since the early 1970s. Clozapine was
considered an “atypical” antipsychotic because it was an effective agent at
doses that caused negligible extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS). Moreover,
it had broad effectiveness for a range of mood and anxiety symptoms that
were common in schizophrenia. This led to a focus on understanding the
mechanism of action of clozapine. Clozapine’s D2 receptor blockade is
lower than that of traditional antipsychotics, while its antagonism of the 5-

these two receptors led Herbert Meltzer to propose that the distinctive
antipsychotic effect of clozapine was related to its low receptor blockade

among the highest for antipsychotic agents.

EUFEST compared several dopamine–serotonin blockers, olanzapine,
quetiapine, ziprasidone with a low dose (1 to 4 mg) of the high-potency
Dopamine D2 blockers haloperidol and amisulpride in the treatment of
first-episode schizophrenia. The pragmatic trial found high-discontinuation
rates 
(highest 
with 
haloperidol), 
and 
symptom 
reductions 
and
rehospitalization rates were virtually the same in all groups. Alongside
olanzapine, amisulpride had the lowest rates of discontinuation for any
reason across an entire year. The results of these trials do not mean that
older and newer antipsychotics are equivalent in their side-effect profiles.
The differences in EPS liability may have been underestimated in CATIE.
First, eliminating patients with evidence of TD may have excluded those
who were most vulnerable to discomforting EPS side effects. Moreover,
while there were no differences in EPS ratings for parkinsonism and
akathisia between perphenazine and the SGAs, it is interesting to note
that the higher rate of discontinuations for EPS among the perphenazine-
treated patients suggests that ratings may not have been adequately
sensitive. However, most of the studies documenting large differences
between these drugs may have used what would now be considered
excessive doses of haloperidol, a drug with an incidence of EPS, which
may have exaggerated the difference between the two types of agents.
The current body evidence does not support the earlier belief that the
dopamine–serotonin or dopamine–serotonin–norepinephrine blockers are
more effective than dopamine D2 blockers. However, the dopamine D2
blockers are more likely to cause EPS and, as noted below, are probably
more likely to cause TD. Perhaps dopamine D2 blockers should be
prescribed in lower dosages than historical uses. If patients are treated
with dopamine D2 blockers, they should be regularly monitored for EPS,
particularly drug-induced parkinsonism and akathisia, and they should be
assessed for evidence of TD.
Maintenance Treatment in Schizophrenia and Schizoaffective
Disorders
Dopamine D2 blockers are effective in decreasing the risk of psychotic
relapse in patients who have recovered from a psychotic episode.
National and international guidelines indicate that after the acute phase of
treatment for a first episode, treatment should continue for at least 1 year,
but there is no consensus regarding the total duration of treatment, if the
patient remains symptomatic. In case of multiple episodes, maintenance

ziprasidone, aripiprazole, iloperidone, lurasidone, zotepine, iloperidone,
amisulpride, at this time) has complicated the decision-making process.
These agents, in themselves quite heterogeneous, have different side-
effect profiles when compared with dopamine blockers. The most
important advantage of these “newer agents” is that they cause
substantially less EPS. Patients who experience EPS at dosages of
dopamine blocker needed to treat their psychosis may or may not
experience EPS with an effective dosage of any of these other agents.
This was evaluated in a phase of the CATIE trial in which patients who
discontinued perphenazine were subsequently randomized to risperidone,
olanzapine, or quetiapine.
There is also evidence from a number of well-designed clinical trials
indicating that patients who have only partial responses to a dopamine
blocker due to lack of efficacy or side effects may improve, if changed to a
dopamine–serotonin and dopamine–serotonin–norepinephrine antagonist.
The evidence is compelling for clozapine, but there are also some reports
supportive of other agents as well. However, most of the studies reporting
this advantage of newer drugs were carried out in the late 1980s and
1990s when patients had only been exposed to dopamine D2 blockers.
More recently, there are clinical reports of patients who had only received
dopamine–serotonin or dopamine–serotonin–norepinephrine antagonists
who improved when they were changed to a dopamine D2 blocker.
Moreover, cost considerations have become more important, especially in
the United States. Many of the newer medications are patent protected
and are considerably more expensive than dopamine blockers which are
usually available as generics. Risks and benefits need to be considered
carefully when choosing antipsychotics, especially in light of the different
TD risks.
An additional advantage of some newer medications is that they are
less likely to elevate prolactin. As a result, these agents may be helpful for
women who experience galactorrhea and irregular menses with dopamine
blockers.
Haloperidol and fluphenazine are still commonly prescribed. They are
more strongly antidopaminergic and thus more likely to cause EPS than
other available medications. However, EPS in some individuals may be
easier to manage than the sedation and orthostatic hypotension
associated with other medications. Haloperidol and Prolixin can also
readily be administered intramuscularly and seldom cause problems with

NEUROLEPTIC MALIGNANT SYNDROME. Risperidone and paliperidone have
been associated with NMS, possibly at rates higher than most other
antipsychotic medications. NMS is a serious and potentially life-
threatening condition. Patients with suspected cases of NMS should be
immediately discontinued from the antipsychotic agent and aggressively
treated with supportive measures, symptomatic treatment, and medical
monitoring. If the patient requires antipsychotic treatment after recovery
from NMS, close monitoring and gradual reintroduction are essential.
CEREBROVASCULAR ADVERSE EVENTS. In placebo-controlled trials, older
adult patients with dementia-related psychosis treated with risperidone
had significantly higher incidences of cerebrovascular accidents and other
related adverse events than did patients treated with placebo.
TARDIVE DYSKINESIA. All antipsychotic medications (with the possible
exceptions of clozapine and quetiapine) carry a risk of tardive dyskinesia.
Tardive dyskinesia risk is thought to be related to a combination of factors,
the most important of which is unopposed D2 blockade in the basal
ganglia. Risperidone has a high affinity for D2 receptors, but its action at
the 5-HT2A receptors may partially mitigate some of the striatal D2
blockade. In one trial of risperidone treatment, 5 of 453 patients
developed symptoms of tardive dyskinesia, and 14 patients with pre-
existing tardive dyskinesia improved. In another study of risperidone
microspheres, the rate of tardive dyskinesia emergence in 530 patients
after 50 weeks of treatment was 1.19%. A review article that considered
the second-generation medications together reported a rate of tardive
dyskinesia with risperidone, amisulpride (Solian), olanzapine, and
quetiapine ranging from 0.5% to 1.5%. The rates of tardive dyskinesia
emergence are slightly higher in older adult populations, especially among
women. Among 133 older adults administered risperidone, the incidence
of persistent tardive dyskinesia was 2.6%, and at doses of 0.75 to 1.5 mg
per day, the incidence dropped to 1%.
HYPERCHOLESTEROLEMIA, 
HYPERGLYCEMIA, 
AND 
DIABETES 
MELLITUS.
Risperidone and paliperidone are associated with weight gain,
dyslipidemias as well as an increased risk of diabetes mellitus. Results
from the CATIE study indicate that risperidone produced changes in
glucose level comparable to perphenazine and quetiapine, with an

as a 5-HT2 antagonist (inverse agonist) that could be added to a D2
antagonist to decrease the amount of extrapyramidal side effects.
Although ritanserin had antinegative symptom effects, improved sleep,
and some weak antipsychotic effects, it also had significant effects on QTc
interval. The synthesis of risperidone in 1984 led the company to focus on
the development of this agent since it combined strong D2 and 5-HT2
antagonism. Subsequent safety and efficacy studies with risperidone led
to its approval in the United States in 1994. This was followed by the
introduction of olanzapine in 1996 and quetiapine in 1997, and others
during the subsequent years. This chapter will discuss the DSAs using the
following NbN categories:
1. Dopamine, serotonin (chlorpromazine, flupenthixol, loxapine,
lurasidone, olanzapine, perospirone, pipotiazine, sertindole,
thioridazine, trifluoperazine, zotepine)
2. Dopamine, serotonin NE α2 (clozapine, risperidone, paliperidone)
3. Dopamine, serotonin, NET (quetiapine)
4. Serotonin, dopamine (iloperidone)
5. Serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine (asenapine)
6. Serotonin, dopamine, serotonin transporter (lumateperone)
The partial agonists, aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, and cariprazine are
discussed in the next chapter.
Comparisons of DSAs
A network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials compared the
effectiveness of 32 antipsychotics. The study found that clozapine,
amisulpride, zotepine, olanzapine, and risperidone were more effective for
improving overall symptoms than other antipsychotics. However, with the
exception of clozapine, the differences between the drugs were relatively
small, and it was not clear that the DSAs were more effective than the
DAs. The differences among the antipsychotics in side effects were
substantial. A reasonable conclusion from this and other meta-analyses is
that—aside from clozapine—the selection of an antipsychotic will be
based on side-effect concerns rather than efficacy.
DOPAMINE, SEROTONIN

This group of agents is similar in structure to the butyrophenones.
Pimozide (Orap), the only diphenylbutylpiperidine available in the United
States (indication solely for Tourette syndrome), is derived from the
butyrophenone benperidol. It has a long half-life: 20 to 26 hours. Doses of
20 mg or higher are associated with seizure risk and QTc prolongation.
This agent has been removed from the market for psychotic conditions
because of those reasons. Penfluridol (Semap) and fluspirilene
(experimental) are antipsychotics from this group that are not available in
the United States.
Benzamides
NbN–amisulpiride, sulpiride
Amisulpride (Solian), a sulfur-containing benzamide, has an unusual
property in that at lower doses (100 mg to 300 mg a day), it tends to
stimulate rather than block dopamine release, producing antidepressant
effects, rendering it potentially useful for the treatment of schizophrenia
patients with negative symptoms. At higher, standard doses, amisulpride
may not have any direct effects on negative symptoms. Amisulpride was
not approved by the Food and Drug Administration for use in the United
States until February 2020, but it has been used in Europe, Israel, Mexico,
India, New Zealand, and Australia to treat psychosis and schizophrenia.
Its current U.S. approval is as an intravenous infusion for postoperative
nausea and vomiting (10-mg dose).
Thioxanthenes
This group shares a similar three-ring structure with the phenothiazines
but has a carbon atom substituted for nitrogen at position 10.
Chlorprothixene 
(Taractan) 
is 
an 
effective 
low-potency 
aliphatic
thioxanthene agent with an antipsychotic potency and a side-effect profile
similar to its phenothiazine counterpart, chlorpromazine. Thiothixene
(Navane), clopenthixol (Sordinol), and flupenthixol (Depixol) are
thioxanthenes with a piperazine substitution. Again, their clinical
characteristics resemble those of their phenothiazine counterparts. As a
result of their double bond at position 10, these agents have geometric
isomers, with the cis isomers demonstrating greater antipsychotic activity.

Dopamine-serotonin antagonists (DSAs) are the most widely prescribed
agents for schizophrenia and other illnesses associated with psychotic
symptoms.
This diverse group of compounds can be differentiated from the
dopamine receptor antagonists based on their high affinity for serotonin
2A (5-HT2A) as well as dopamine (D2) receptors. In prior editions of this
text, the term second-generation antipsychotics or SGAs was used to
refer to these agents. However, this term is inaccurate since decades of
studies have failed to support the contention that antipsychotics marketed
after clozapine were more effective antipsychotics than older drugs. The
adoption of neuroscience-based nomenclature (NbN) provides a preferred
method for characterizing antipsychotic medications based on their
pharmacology. It is notable that antipsychotics previously considered first-
generation antipsychotics—including chlorpromazine, thioridazine, and
flupenthixol—are categorized as DSAs, and sulpiride and amisulpride are
classified as dopamine antagonists (DAs).
The differentiation of the DSAs from other antipsychotics emerged
following the introduction of clozapine (Clozaril), an antipsychotic that was
introduced in the United States in 1990, although it had been available in
some countries in Europe since the early 1970s. Clozapine was
considered an “atypical” antipsychotic because it was an effective agent at
doses that caused negligible extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS). Moreover,
it had broad effectiveness for a range of mood and anxiety symptoms that
were common in schizophrenia. This led to a focus on understanding the
mechanism of action of clozapine. Clozapine’s D2 receptor blockade is
lower than that of traditional antipsychotics, while its antagonism of the 5-
HT2 receptor is greater than that of haloperidol. The unique activity at
these two receptors led Herbert Meltzer to propose that the distinctive
antipsychotic effect of clozapine was related to its low receptor blockade
at D2 relative to 5-HT2. Clozapine’s affinity for the 5-HT2 receptor is
among the highest for antipsychotic agents.
During the early 1980s, scientists at Janssen Pharmaceutica were
interested in developing an antipsychotic that would have a clinical profile
similar to clozapine but without a tendency to cause agranulocytosis. The
company developed a number of drugs with 5-HT2 antagonism with and
without D2 activity. One compound, setoperone, had weak dopamine
activity and was a relatively weak antipsychotic. Ritanserin was developed

Acute Psychosis
Numerous double-blind clinical trials have demonstrated that dopamine
D2 blockers are more effective than placebo for reducing symptoms of
psychosis. The initial studies were carried out in the 1960s by the NIMH,
reviewed by Donald Klein and John Davis, who concluded that with the
exception of mepazine (Pacatal) and promazine, all of these agents were
effective. These and subsequent studies also demonstrated that
antipsychotics are effective for every subgroup of patients with
schizophrenia. In 2009, the Schizophrenia Patient Outcomes Research
Team (PORT) updated prior reviews and concluded that there is clear
evidence that dopamine D2 blockers are effective for reducing positive
symptoms during acute psychotic episodes. PORT recommendations also
suggest that choosing antipsychotics should be based on individual
preference, prior treatment response and adherence history, medical
history and risk factors, the individual medication’s side-effect profile, and
long-term treatment planning. Studies found that amisulpride can be
safely administered at an optimal dose immediately, not needing a titration
phase and thereby aiding in acute symptom control.

are effective in reducing psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations and
paranoid ideation, to a greater extent than anxiety and depression.

Efficacy may be dose-related: lower doses may help negative symptoms, while higher doses may be needed for positive symptoms.

answer.explanation:
Evidence for effectiveness: Stahl states that amisulpride most often reduces positive symptoms in schizophrenia and can improve negative, aggressive, cognitive, and affective symptoms; it also notes that efficacy for negative symptoms may be achieved at lower doses while positive symptoms may require higher doses. Stahl further notes that efficacy has been particularly well demonstrated in patients with predominantly negative symptoms. Kaplan reports that in EUFEST, amisulpride (low-dose high-potency D2 blocker) produced symptom reductions and rehospitalization rates that were virtually the same as comparator antipsychotics, with low discontinuation rates. NbN also lists schizophrenia (UK/France), negative symptoms of schizophrenia, and improvement of psychotic symptoms as efficacy/indication statements.

Structure-mechanism link: Stahl explicitly classifies amisulpride as an atypical antipsychotic (benzamide) and a dopamine receptor antagonist. Stahl also describes a theoretical dose-dependent mechanism: presynaptic D2 blockade at low doses and postsynaptic D2 blockade at higher doses, with possible D3 blockade and minimal potent serotonin 2A/1A activity. NbN similarly identifies amisulpride as a dopamine antagonist, with pre-synaptic antagonist mode of action, D2/D3 antagonism, and no significant 5-HT2A binding on PET. Together, these sources support that the benzamide structure is associated with a dopamine-receptor-antagonist profile rather than a serotonin-dominant one.
answer.direct_answer: Amisulpride has evidence of antipsychotic efficacy in schizophrenia, including improvement in positive symptoms and negative symptoms; in the EUFEST first-episode schizophrenia trial, symptom reduction and rehospitalization were virtually the same as with comparator antipsychotics, and amisulpride had among the lowest discontinuation rates. Its benzamide structure is reflected in its classification as an atypical antipsychotic (benzamide) and its mechanism as a dopamine receptor antagonist, with low-dose presynaptic D2 blockade and higher-dose postsynaptic D2 blockade; it also blocks D3 receptors and has little potent 5-HT2A/5-HT1A activity.

Acute Psychosis
Numerous double-blind clinical trials have demonstrated that dopamine
D2 blockers are more effective than placebo for reducing symptoms of

Dopamine D2 blockers are effective in decreasing the risk of psychotic

Acute Psychosis
Numerous double-blind clinical trials have demonstrated that dopamine
D2 blockers are more effective than placebo for reducing symptoms of
psychosis. The initial studies were carried out in the 1960s by the NIMH,
reviewed by Donald Klein and John Davis, who concluded that with the
exception of mepazine (Pacatal) and promazine, all of these agents were
effective. These and subsequent studies also demonstrated that
antipsychotics are effective for every subgroup of patients with
schizophrenia. In 2009, the Schizophrenia Patient Outcomes Research
Team (PORT) updated prior reviews and concluded that there is clear
evidence that dopamine D2 blockers are effective for reducing positive
symptoms during acute psychotic episodes. PORT recommendations also
suggest that choosing antipsychotics should be based on individual
preference, prior treatment response and adherence history, medical
history and risk factors, the individual medication’s side-effect profile, and
long-term treatment planning. Studies found that amisulpride can be
safely administered at an optimal dose immediately, not needing a titration

answer.explanation: The Kaplan passage states that EUFEST compared olanzapine, quetiapine, ziprasidone, haloperidol, and amisulpride in first-episode schizophrenia, and that the pragmatic trial found high discontinuation rates overall, with the highest discontinuation on haloperidol. Acute Psychosis
Numerous double-blind clinical trials have demonstrated that dopamine
D2 blockers are more effective than placebo for reducing symptoms of
psychosis. The initial studies were carried out in the 1960s by the NIMH,
reviewed by Donald Klein and John Davis, who concluded that with the
exception of mepazine (Pacatal) and promazine, all of these agents were
effective. These and subsequent studies also demonstrated that
antipsychotics are effective for every subgroup of patients with
schizophrenia. In 2009, the Schizophrenia Patient Outcomes Research
Team (PORT) updated prior reviews and concluded that there is clear
evidence that dopamine D2 blockers are effective for reducing positive
symptoms during acute psychotic episodes. PORT recommendations also
suggest that choosing antipsychotics should be based on individual
preference, prior treatment response and adherence history, medical

Dopamine-serotonin antagonists (DSAs) are the most widely prescribed
agents for schizophrenia and other illnesses associated with psychotic
symptoms.
This diverse group of compounds can be differentiated from the
dopamine receptor antagonists based on their high affinity for serotonin
2A (5-HT2A) as well as dopamine (D2) receptors. In prior editions of this
text, the term second-generation antipsychotics or SGAs was used to
refer to these agents. However, this term is inaccurate since decades of
studies have failed to support the contention that antipsychotics marketed
after clozapine were more effective antipsychotics than older drugs. The
adoption of neuroscience-based nomenclature (NbN) provides a preferred
method for characterizing antipsychotic medications based on their
pharmacology. It is notable that antipsychotics previously considered first-
generation antipsychotics—including chlorpromazine, thioridazine, and
flupenthixol—are categorized as DSAs, and sulpiride and amisulpride are
classified as dopamine antagonists (DAs).
The differentiation of the DSAs from other antipsychotics emerged
following the introduction of clozapine (Clozaril), an antipsychotic that was
introduced in the United States in 1990, although it had been available in
some countries in Europe since the early 1970s. Clozapine was
considered an “atypical” antipsychotic because it was an effective agent at
doses that caused negligible extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS). Moreover,
it had broad effectiveness for a range of mood and anxiety symptoms that
were common in schizophrenia. This led to a focus on understanding the
mechanism of action of clozapine. Clozapine’s D2 receptor blockade is
lower than that of traditional antipsychotics, while its antagonism of the 5-
HT2 receptor is greater than that of haloperidol. The unique activity at
these two receptors led Herbert Meltzer to propose that the distinctive
antipsychotic effect of clozapine was related to its low receptor blockade
at D2 relative to 5-HT2. Clozapine’s affinity for the 5-HT2 receptor is
among the highest for antipsychotic agents.
During the early 1980s, scientists at Janssen Pharmaceutica were
interested in developing an antipsychotic that would have a clinical profile
similar to clozapine but without a tendency to cause agranulocytosis. The
company developed a number of drugs with 5-HT2 antagonism with and
without D2 activity. One compound, setoperone, had weak dopamine

antagonists remain the most commonly prescribed antipsychotics in many
parts of the world, and as cost considerations have become more
prominent, dopamine D2 receptor antagonists remain frequently

These agents are highly effective for nearly all disorders that result in
psychotic symptoms. However, these drugs have important limitations:
They can cause acute and chronic neurologic symptoms that, especially
at higher doses, significantly limit their effectiveness; they are ineffective
or only partially effective for a substantial proportion of psychotic patients;
the minimally effective dosage has frequently not been determined, and

efficacy for some of the most important signs and symptoms of the most
common psychotic illness, schizophrenia. In higher dosages, the motor
symptoms may induce “secondary” negative symptoms, such as akinesia,
emotional blunting, apathy, and cognitive impairment.

answer.explanation: The provided clinical-trial evidence comes from EUFEST, which compared low-dose haloperidol and amisulpride among other antipsychotics in first-episode schizophrenia. The trial found that symptom reductions and rehospitalization rates were virtually the same across groups, but discontinuation was highest with haloperidol. Amisulpride, alongside olanzapine, had the lowest discontinuation rates for any reason. No other head-to-head trial details are provided in the evidence package. [kaplan_chunk_904]

Dopamine-serotonin antagonists (DSAs) are the most widely prescribed
agents for schizophrenia and other illnesses associated with psychotic
symptoms.
This diverse group of compounds can be differentiated from the
dopamine receptor antagonists based on their high affinity for serotonin
2A (5-HT2A) as well as dopamine (D2) receptors. In prior editions of this
text, the term second-generation antipsychotics or SGAs was used to
refer to these agents. However, this term is inaccurate since decades of
studies have failed to support the contention that antipsychotics marketed
after clozapine were more effective antipsychotics than older drugs. The
adoption of neuroscience-based nomenclature (NbN) provides a preferred
method for characterizing antipsychotic medications based on their
pharmacology. It is notable that antipsychotics previously considered first-
generation antipsychotics—including chlorpromazine, thioridazine, and
flupenthixol—are categorized as DSAs, and sulpiride and amisulpride are
classified as dopamine antagonists (DAs).
The differentiation of the DSAs from other antipsychotics emerged
following the introduction of clozapine (Clozaril), an antipsychotic that was
introduced in the United States in 1990, although it had been available in
some countries in Europe since the early 1970s. Clozapine was
considered an “atypical” antipsychotic because it was an effective agent at
doses that caused negligible extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS). Moreover,
it had broad effectiveness for a range of mood and anxiety symptoms that
were common in schizophrenia. This led to a focus on understanding the
mechanism of action of clozapine. Clozapine’s D2 receptor blockade is
lower than that of traditional antipsychotics, while its antagonism of the 5-
HT2 receptor is greater than that of haloperidol. The unique activity at
these two receptors led Herbert Meltzer to propose that the distinctive
antipsychotic effect of clozapine was related to its low receptor blockade
at D2 relative to 5-HT2. Clozapine’s affinity for the 5-HT2 receptor is
among the highest for antipsychotic agents.
During the early 1980s, scientists at Janssen Pharmaceutica were
interested in developing an antipsychotic that would have a clinical profile
similar to clozapine but without a tendency to cause agranulocytosis. The
company developed a number of drugs with 5-HT2 antagonism with and
without D2 activity. One compound, setoperone, had weak dopamine
activity and was a relatively weak antipsychotic. Ritanserin was developed

as a 5-HT2 antagonist (inverse agonist) that could be added to a D2
antagonist to decrease the amount of extrapyramidal side effects.
Although ritanserin had antinegative symptom effects, improved sleep,
and some weak antipsychotic effects, it also had significant effects on QTc
interval. The synthesis of risperidone in 1984 led the company to focus on
the development of this agent since it combined strong D2 and 5-HT2
antagonism. Subsequent safety and efficacy studies with risperidone led
to its approval in the United States in 1994. This was followed by the
introduction of olanzapine in 1996 and quetiapine in 1997, and others
during the subsequent years. This chapter will discuss the DSAs using the
following NbN categories:
1. Dopamine, serotonin (chlorpromazine, flupenthixol, loxapine,
lurasidone, olanzapine, perospirone, pipotiazine, sertindole,
thioridazine, trifluoperazine, zotepine)
2. Dopamine, serotonin NE α2 (clozapine, risperidone, paliperidone)
3. Dopamine, serotonin, NET (quetiapine)
4. Serotonin, dopamine (iloperidone)
5. Serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine (asenapine)
6. Serotonin, dopamine, serotonin transporter (lumateperone)
The partial agonists, aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, and cariprazine are
discussed in the next chapter.
Comparisons of DSAs
A network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials compared the
effectiveness of 32 antipsychotics. The study found that clozapine,
amisulpride, zotepine, olanzapine, and risperidone were more effective for
improving overall symptoms than other antipsychotics. However, with the
exception of clozapine, the differences between the drugs were relatively
small, and it was not clear that the DSAs were more effective than the
DAs. The differences among the antipsychotics in side effects were
substantial. A reasonable conclusion from this and other meta-analyses is
that—aside from clozapine—the selection of an antipsychotic will be
based on side-effect concerns rather than efficacy.

answer.explanation: In the NbN evidence, amisulpride is listed under the class "Antipsychotic" and also described mechanistically as a dopamine receptor antagonist, including a presynaptic antagonist and D2/D3 antagonist actions ([nbn_claim_224], [nbn_claim_218], [nbn_claim_236], [nbn_claim_233]). Stahl explicitly gives the NbN class as "dopamine receptor antagonist (D-RAn)" and separately notes the older clinical class label "Atypical antipsychotic (benzamide...)" ([stahl_claim_2101], [stahl_claim_2102]). Kaplan explains that the NbN-style reclassification shifts antipsychotics toward mechanism-based categories, replacing the older first-versus second-generation dichotomy ([kaplan_chunk_879]). So the effect of the NbN reclassification is that amisulpride is categorized by mechanism as a dopamine receptor antagonist, not primarily by the older atypical/second-generation label ([stahl_claim_2101], [kaplan_chunk_879]).
answer.direct_answer: NbN reclassifies amisulpride as a dopamine receptor antagonist (D-RAn), rather than simply an antipsychotic/“atypical antipsychotic.”

Dopamine-serotonin antagonists (DSAs) are the most widely prescribed
agents for schizophrenia and other illnesses associated with psychotic
symptoms.
This diverse group of compounds can be differentiated from the
dopamine receptor antagonists based on their high affinity for serotonin

studies have failed to support the contention that antipsychotics marketed

adoption of neuroscience-based nomenclature (NbN) provides a preferred
method for characterizing antipsychotic medications based on their
pharmacology. It is notable that antipsychotics previously considered first-

flupenthixol—are categorized as DSAs, and sulpiride and amisulpride are
classified as dopamine antagonists (DAs).
The differentiation of the DSAs from other antipsychotics emerged
following the introduction of clozapine (Clozaril), an antipsychotic that was
introduced in the United States in 1990, although it had been available in
some countries in Europe since the early 1970s. Clozapine was
considered an “atypical” antipsychotic because it was an effective agent at
doses that caused negligible extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS). Moreover,
it had broad effectiveness for a range of mood and anxiety symptoms that
were common in schizophrenia. This led to a focus on understanding the
mechanism of action of clozapine. Clozapine’s D2 receptor blockade is
lower than that of traditional antipsychotics, while its antagonism of the 5-
HT2 receptor is greater than that of haloperidol. The unique activity at
these two receptors led Herbert Meltzer to propose that the distinctive
antipsychotic effect of clozapine was related to its low receptor blockade
at D2 relative to 5-HT2. Clozapine’s affinity for the 5-HT2 receptor is
among the highest for antipsychotic agents.

answer.direct_answer: For first-episode schizophrenia, amisulpride can be used as an antipsychotic at standard schizophrenia doses, with evidence from first-episode trials showing similar symptom reduction and rehospitalization outcomes to comparator antipsychotics; in practice, it should be started at an intermediate dose and titrated over 3–7 days, with long-term treatment continued at least 1 year after the first episode once a satisfactory plateau is reached. Dopamine-serotonin antagonists (DSAs) are the most widely prescribed
agents for schizophrenia and other illnesses associated with psychotic
symptoms.
This diverse group of compounds can be differentiated from the
dopamine receptor antagonists based on their high affinity for serotonin
2A (5-HT2A) as well as dopamine (D2) receptors. In prior editions of this
text, the term second-generation antipsychotics or SGAs was used to
refer to these agents. However, this term is inaccurate since decades of
studies have failed to support the contention that antipsychotics marketed
after clozapine were more effective antipsychotics than older drugs. The
adoption of neuroscience-based nomenclature (NbN) provides a preferred
method for characterizing antipsychotic medications based on their
pharmacology. It is notable that antipsychotics previously considered first-
generation antipsychotics—including chlorpromazine, thioridazine, and
flupenthixol—are categorized as DSAs, and sulpiride and amisulpride are
classified as dopamine antagonists (DAs).
The differentiation of the DSAs from other antipsychotics emerged
following the introduction of clozapine (Clozaril), an antipsychotic that was
introduced in the United States in 1990, although it had been available in
some countries in Europe since the early 1970s. Clozapine was
considered an “atypical” antipsychotic because it was an effective agent at
doses that caused negligible extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS). Moreover,
it had broad effectiveness for a range of mood and anxiety symptoms that
were common in schizophrenia. This led to a focus on understanding the
mechanism of action of clozapine. Clozapine’s D2 receptor blockade is
lower than that of traditional antipsychotics, while its antagonism of the 5-
HT2 receptor is greater than that of haloperidol. The unique activity at
these two receptors led Herbert Meltzer to propose that the distinctive
antipsychotic effect of clozapine was related to its low receptor blockade
at D2 relative to 5-HT2. Clozapine’s affinity for the 5-HT2 receptor is
among the highest for antipsychotic agents.
During the early 1980s, scientists at Janssen Pharmaceutica were
interested in developing an antipsychotic that would have a clinical profile
similar to clozapine but without a tendency to cause agranulocytosis. The
company developed a number of drugs with 5-HT2 antagonism with and
without D2 activity. One compound, setoperone, had weak dopamine
activity and was a relatively weak antipsychotic. Ritanserin was developed

as a 5-HT2 antagonist (inverse agonist) that could be added to a D2
antagonist to decrease the amount of extrapyramidal side effects.
Although ritanserin had antinegative symptom effects, improved sleep,
and some weak antipsychotic effects, it also had significant effects on QTc
interval. The synthesis of risperidone in 1984 led the company to focus on
the development of this agent since it combined strong D2 and 5-HT2
antagonism. Subsequent safety and efficacy studies with risperidone led
to its approval in the United States in 1994. This was followed by the
introduction of olanzapine in 1996 and quetiapine in 1997, and others
during the subsequent years. This chapter will discuss the DSAs using the
following NbN categories:
1. Dopamine, serotonin (chlorpromazine, flupenthixol, loxapine,
lurasidone, olanzapine, perospirone, pipotiazine, sertindole,
thioridazine, trifluoperazine, zotepine)
2. Dopamine, serotonin NE α2 (clozapine, risperidone, paliperidone)
3. Dopamine, serotonin, NET (quetiapine)
4. Serotonin, dopamine (iloperidone)
5. Serotonin, dopamine, norepinephrine (asenapine)
6. Serotonin, dopamine, serotonin transporter (lumateperone)
The partial agonists, aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, and cariprazine are
discussed in the next chapter.
Comparisons of DSAs
A network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials compared the
effectiveness of 32 antipsychotics. The study found that clozapine,
amisulpride, zotepine, olanzapine, and risperidone were more effective for
improving overall symptoms than other antipsychotics. However, with the
exception of clozapine, the differences between the drugs were relatively
small, and it was not clear that the DSAs were more effective than the
DAs. The differences among the antipsychotics in side effects were
substantial. A reasonable conclusion from this and other meta-analyses is
that—aside from clozapine—the selection of an antipsychotic will be
based on side-effect concerns rather than efficacy.
DOPAMINE, SEROTONIN

citations.text: NbN lists amisulpride as an antipsychotic but also specifies its neuroscience-based mechanism as a dopamine receptor antagonist, including presynaptic D2 antagonism and D2/D3 antagonism.
Stahl categorizes amisulpride in NbN terms as a dopamine receptor antagonist (D-RAn) and also describes it as an atypical antipsychotic.
Kaplan states that the old first-versus second-generation antipsychotic division is obsolete and that mechanism-based terms such as dopamine–receptor antagonists are used instead.

answer.explanation: In the NbN evidence, amisulpride is listed under the class “Antipsychotic,” but the more specific NbN mechanism is “dopamine receptor antagonist (D-RAn)” with D2/D3 antagonism and presynaptic D2 antagonism noted. Stahl likewise labels it as a “Neuroscience-based Nomenclature: dopamine receptor antagonist (D-RAn)” and describes it as an atypical antipsychotic, showing the reclassification shifts emphasis from the older antipsychotic category to a mechanism-based dopamine receptor antagonist category. Kaplan supports this broader NbN shift by stating that the old first-versus second-generation antipsychotic division is obsolete and that mechanism-based terms such as dopamine–receptor antagonists are now used.
answer.direct_answer: NbN reclassifies amisulpride as a dopamine receptor antagonist (D-RAn), rather than simply an antipsychotic/“atypical antipsychotic.”
